chunks: Ali ibn al-Hasan ibn Fadhal narrated from Muhammad ibn Abdillah from Muhammad ibn Aslam from Yunus ibn Abi al-Harith from Saif ibn Umaira from Mansur ibn Hazim, who said:

I heard Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) saying: 'The mawla (client) of the daughter of Hamza died, and he had a daughter. So the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) gave the daughter of Hamza half [of the estate] and her daughter half [of the estate].'

Muhammad ibn al-Hasan said: This is a report on which action is not taken, because it agrees with the schools of the general public (Sunni), and it has come out as a form of precautionary dissimulation (taqiyyah) due to its contradiction with the reports we have previously mentioned. And because this is a report that they (the Sunnis) narrate from the Prophet (peace be upon him and his family), so it is permissible that it comes in accordance with what they believe, namely that it has been narrated that the Prophet (peace be upon him and his family) gave all the wealth to the daughter of Hamza because she had no heir.

key_terms.ابْنَةُ حَمْزَةَ: Daughter of Hamza, referring to the daughter of the Prophet's paternal uncle, Hamza ibn Abd al-Muttalib.
key_terms.التَّقِيَّة: Taqiyyah (precautionary dissimulation), the practice of concealing one's true beliefs or rulings to avoid harm or conflict.
key_terms.الْعَامَّة: Al-Ammah (the general public), often referring to Sunni Muslims in contrast to the Shia.
key_terms.مَوْلًى: Mawla (client/freedman), a person who enters into a patronage relationship with a tribe or individual.
key_terms.وَارِث: Warith (heir), one who inherits property or status from the deceased.

ai.seo_question: How is the estate of a mawla distributed between the daughter of Hamza and the mawla's own daughter according to Shia and Sunni traditions?
ai.summary: This narration from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* illustrates the distribution of a mawla's estate between the daughter of Hamza and the deceased's daughter, a ruling accepted by Sunnis but treated with caution in Shia jurisprudence. Shaykh al-Tusi’s commentator, Ibn al-Hassan, classifies it as *taqiyyah* (dissimulation) because it contradicts the stronger Shia position that the daughter of Hamza inherits the entire estate as the sole heir when no direct descendants exist. This highlights the methodological distinction between accepting a report for its narrative value versus adopting it as a binding legal precedent.
